extracted.intended_audience: artists, critics, and educated readers interested in standards for evaluating literature and the arts
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging whether a work of art (poetry, prose, painting, music, drama) is truly artistic — with emphasis on intelligibility, sincerity, universality, and emotional transmission rather than deliberate obscurity or elitist novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensibility / intelligibility to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Art should be intelligible; its language should be understood by all and should act on people independently of their education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy asserts that great works transmit feelings that are comprehensible to everyone (examples: the Gospel parables, folk-legends, the Iliad/Odyssey). He criticizes modern works that are 'absolutely unintelligible' (samples from Baudelaire, Verlaine, Mallarmé, Maeterlinck) as failing this test. Anti-patterns: deliberate obscurity, puzzle-like versification that leaves readers unable to tell who is speaking or what is happening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of deliberate obscurity / mystery-as-dogma
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscurity, haziness, and a cultivated 'mystery' are not virtues in themselves and should not be elevated to a dogma of poetic art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy quotes and critiques Verlaine and Mallarmé who advocate suggestion and allusion over naming; he labels the 'theory of obscurity' as a new dogma among the Decadents. Examples given: Petits Poèmes en Prose requiring to 'guess like a rebus'; Mallarmé's injunction that 'there should always be an enigma' are presented as anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional transmission (infectiousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary business of art is to make feeling understood and felt — to 'infect' people with emotion across social and cultural boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy insists art should 'infect any man whatever his plane of development' and contrasts this with technical or intellectual activity requiring special preparation. Works that produce only weariness (e.g., abstruse music or gymnastic piano exercises) fail because they do not transmit feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality / accessibility rather than elitist exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Good art addresses and moves broad masses of people rather than being intelligible only to an elect or an inner circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy rejects the modern claim that a work can be 'very good but very difficult to understand' for the masses; he condemns the attitude 'I create and understand myself, and if anyone does not understand me, so much the worse for him.' Examples: Decadent preference for art 'accessible only to the elect' is criticized as ruinous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity, naïveté, and simplicity (absence of artificiality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art should exhibit sincerity, simplicity, and naïveté rather than artificiality, forced originality, or self-assurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy criticizes Baudelaire and Verlaine for lacking 'naïveté, sincerity, and simplicity' and overflowing with artificiality and 'forced originality.' Anti-patterns: works in which you 'see more of M. Baudelaire or M. Verlaine than of what they were describing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/ethical direction of feeling (avoidance of gross egotism and pornographic detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject-matter and feelings communicated by art should be elevated rather than low, perverted, or grossly egotistical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy condemns Baudelaire's elevation of 'gross egotism' and the use of 'hitherto unused pornographic details' to freshen form. Anti-patterns include poems whose feelings are 'evil and very low ones' and the substitution of morality by 'a cloudy conception of beauty.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, eloquence, passion, and truth in expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and other art ought not to banish eloquence, passion, and truth; these are valuable qualities in expressive art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy cites Gautier noting that Baudelaire 'banished ... eloquence, the passion, and the truth too strictly copied' and treats that banishment as a negative. Anti-pattern: treating eloquence/passion/truth as defects to be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness and coherence of imagery, metaphors, and comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagery and comparisons should be coherent, intelligible, and not incorrect or gratuitously obscure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy points to lines like 'How can snow shine like sand?' or 'The moon seem to live and die in a copper heaven?' as examples of incorrect comparisons that produce unintelligibility rather than impression. Anti-pattern: strings of 'incorrect comparisons and words' masquerading as impressionistic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and subject-matter competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Good art requires skilful form and worthy subject-matter; poor form or commonplace subject-matter undermines a work's value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy criticizes entire sections (e.g., Verlaine's 'La Sagesse') for poor expression, trite patriotic or religious sentiment badly expressed, and weak formal skill. Anti-patterns: verses 'far from skilful in form and most contemptible and commonplace in subject-matter.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding novelty-for-novelty's-sake and amusement-refreshing
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventing new forms merely to 'freshen up' an amusement-driven art is not a criterion of true artistic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy analogizes upper-class art to games that need novelty when they become wearying (whist → écarté → other novelty). He argues Decadents invent new forms and tack on pornographic details to make stale amusement tolerable; such novelty does not equal greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference from intellectual activity requiring preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is distinct from intellectual exercises that demand special training; where the latter require preparatory knowledge, art should still move the untrained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy contrasts art with activities like trigonometry that require prior knowledge. He argues true art 'acts on people independently of their state of development and education.' Anti-pattern: works that require specialist 'preparation' to be appreciated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation must be genuine, not habituation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a work is said to be hard to understand, the explanation must actually convey the necessary knowledge; telling people to 'read it over and over' is mere habituation, not explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy warns that defenders of difficult art often only say 'one must read, and see, and hear these same works over and over again' — which he calls habituation, comparable to habituation to bad food or opium, and not a true explanation that produces understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-medium intelligibility (poetry, painting, music, drama, prose all must communicate)
rubrics_metrics.description: All arts — painting, music, drama, novels — should convey clear impressions and move people; incoherence in any medium indicates failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy gives examples across media: paintings with indecipherable subjects and odd colouring; music that is 'gymnastic' but transmits only weariness; dramas and novels where events and motives are unintelligible. Anti-pattern: modern composers/painters/dramatists producing works 'beyond human comprehension.'
